title: Seeing the unseen beyond the heavens
source_text: Ἄντικρυς γὰρ τοῖς ἀκούειν δυναμένοις παρίστησι τὰ μὲν αἰσθητὰ λέγων αὐτὰ „βλεπόμενα,“ τὰ δὲ νοητὰ καὶ νῷ μόνῳ καταληπτὰ ὀνομάζων „μὴ βλεπόμενα.“ οὗτος δὲ καὶ „πρόσκαιρα“ μὲν οἶδε τὰ αἰσθητὰ καὶ „βλεπόμενα,“ „αἰώνια“ δὲ τὰ νοητὰ καὶ „μὴ βλεπόμενα“· καὶ βουλόμενος πρὸς τῇ ἐκείνων θέᾳ γενέσθαι ὑπὸ τοῦ πρὸς ἐκεῖνα πόθου βοηθούμενος πᾶσαν θλῖψιν τὸ οὐδὲν καὶ ἐλαφράν τινα ἐνόμιζεν εἶναι· καὶ παρ᾿ αὐτὸν τὸν „τῆς θλίψεως“ καὶ τῶν πόνων καιρὸν μηδαμῶς μὲν βαρούμενος ὑπ᾿ αὐτῶν, ἐπελαφρίζων δὲ διὰ τὴν περὶ ἐκεῖνα θέαν πᾶσαν περίστασιν· ἐπεὶ καὶ ἔχομεν ἡμεῖς „ἀρχιερέα μέγαν“ τῷ μεγέθει τῆς δυνάμεως καὶ τοῦ νοῦ αὐτοῦ „διεληλυθότα τοὺς οὐρανοὺς, Ἰησοῦν τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ θεοῦ,“ ἐπαγγειλάμενον τοῖς γνησίως μαθοῦσι τὰ θεῖα καὶ ἀξίως αὐτῶν βιώσασι προάξειν αὐτοὺς ἐπὶ τὰ ὑπερκόσμια· φησὶ γάρ· „ἵν᾿ ὅπου ἐγὼ ὑπάγω καὶ ὑμεῖς ἦτε.“ διὰ τοῦτο ἡμεῖς μετὰ τοὺς ἐνταῦθα πόνους καὶ τοὺς ἀγῶνας ἐλπίζομεν πρὸς ἄκροις γενέσθαι τοῖς οὐρανοῖς, καὶ πηγὰς „ὕδατος ἁλλομένου εἰς ζωὴν αἰώνιον“ ἀναλαβόντες κατὰ τὴν Ἰησοῦ διδασκαλίαν ποταμούς τε χωρήσαντες τῶν θεωρημάτων σὺν τοῖς λεγομένοις ὕδασιν „ὑπεράνω τῶν οὐρανῶν.“ αἰνοῦσι „τὸ ὄνομα κυρίου,“ ἔσεσθαι. καὶ ὅσον γε αἰνοῦμεν αὐτὸν, οὐ περιαχθησόμεθα ἀπὸ τῆς τοῦ οὐρανοῦ περιφορᾶς, ἀεὶ δὲ πρὸς τῇ θέᾳ ἐσόμεθα τῶν ἀοράτων τοῦ θεοῦ, οὐκέτι „ἀπὸ κτίσεως κόσμου τοῖς ποιήμασι“ νοουμένων ἡμῖν, ἀλλ᾿ ὡς ὠνόμασεν ὁ γνήσιος τοῦ Ἰησοῦ μαθητὴς λέγων· „τότε δὲ πρόσωπον πρὸς πρόσωπον“ καὶ τό· „ἐὰν ἔλθῃ τὸ τέλειον, τὸ ἐκ μέρους καταργηθήσεται.“
pass_a_gloss: For plainly (ἄντικρυς) to those able to hear he presents (παρίστημι), calling the sensible things (αἰσθητά) 'seen (βλεπόμενα)', and naming the intelligible things (νοητά) and graspable (καταληπτά) by mind alone 'not seen'. And he knows (οἶδα) the sensible and 'seen' things as 'temporary (πρόσκαιρα)', and the intelligible and 'not seen' as 'eternal (αἰώνια)'; and wishing to be at the contemplation (θέα) of those, helped (βοηθέω) by the longing (πόθος) for them, he considered (νομίζω) every affliction (θλῖψις) the nothing and a light (ἐλαφρά) thing; and at the very time (καιρός) 'of affliction' and of toils (πόνοι) in no way being weighed down (βαρέω) by them, but lightening (ἐπελαφρίζω) because of the contemplation of those things every hardship (περίστασις); since also we have 'a great high priest (ἀρχιερεὺς μέγας)' by the greatness of his power (δύναμις) and mind (νοῦς) 'having passed through (διέρχομαι) the heavens, Jesus the Son of God', having promised (ἐπαγγέλλομαι) those who genuinely (γνησίως) learned divine things (τὰ θεῖα) and lived (βιόω) worthily of them to lead them forward (προάγω) to the things beyond the world (ὑπερκόσμια); for he says: 'that where I go (ὑπάγω) you also may be.' Because of this we, after the toils here and the contests (ἀγῶνες), hope (ἐλπίζω) to be at the summits (ἄκρα) of the heavens, and having taken up (ἀναλαμβάνω) springs (πηγαί) 'of water leaping (ἅλλομαι) into eternal life' according to the teaching (διδασκαλία) of Jesus, and having contained (χωρέω) rivers (ποταμοί) of contemplations (θεωρήματα), with the waters said to be 'above the heavens', praising 'the name of the Lord', to be. And as long as we praise him, we shall not be carried around (περιάγω) by the revolution (περιφορά) of heaven, but always we shall be at the contemplation of the invisible things (ἀόρατα) of God, no longer understood (νοέω) by us 'from the creation (κτίσις) of the world by the things made (ποιήματα)', but as the genuine disciple of Jesus named it, saying: 'but then face to face' and: 'if the perfect (τὸ τέλειον) comes, the in-part (τὸ ἐκ μέρους) will be done away (καταργέω).'
pass_b_english: For to those able to hear he states it plainly, calling the things of sense “what is seen,” and naming the intelligible things, grasped by the mind alone, “what is not seen.” He also knows that the things of sense, the things “seen,” are “temporary,” and that the intelligible things, the things “not seen,” are “eternal” (2 Corinthians 4:18). And since he wished to be engaged in contemplating those things, helped by his longing for them he counted every affliction as nothing and as something light. In the very time of “affliction” and toil he was in no way weighed down by them; because of his contemplation of those things he made light of every hardship.

For we too have “a great high priest,” who by the greatness of his power and of his mind “has passed through the heavens, Jesus the Son of God” (Hebrews 4:14). He has promised those who have truly learned divine things and have lived worthily of them that he will lead them on to what lies beyond the world. For he says: “so that where I am going, you also may be” (John 14:3).

For this reason we hope, after the toils and the contests here, to reach the very heights of the heavens. Having received, according to the teaching of Jesus, springs of “water welling up to eternal life” (John 4:14), and having made room for rivers of contemplation (John 7:38), we hope to be with the waters said to be “above the heavens,” which praise “the name of the Lord” (Psalm 148:4–5). And as long as we praise him, we shall not be carried round by the revolving of heaven, but shall always be engaged in contemplating the invisible things of God, no longer understood by us “from the creation of the world through the things that are made” (Romans 1:20), but as the true disciple of Jesus put it, when he said, “but then face to face” (1 Corinthians 13:12), and, “when what is perfect comes, what is partial will be done away” (1 Corinthians 13:10).

choices.choice: The opening sentences comment on 2 Corinthians 4:17–18 quoted at the end of 6.19; the quoted words (‘seen’, ‘not seen’, ‘temporary’, ‘eternal’, ‘affliction’) are from that text, cited inline once as 2 Corinthians 4:18. ‘Where I am going, you also may be’: Origen has ὑπάγω; John 14:3 reads ὅπου εἰμὶ ἐγώ; compare John 14:4 (ὅπου ὑπάγω) and 17:24; cited as John 14:3. ‘Rivers of contemplation’ alludes to John 7:38 (ποταμοὶ … ὕδατος ζῶντος), linked to the John 4:14 springs by ‘according to the teaching of Jesus’; cited as a clear allusion. The TEI prints a full stop before αἰνοῦσι and a comma before ἔσεσθαι; the clause is read as one: we hope ‘to be with (σὺν) the waters above the heavens, which praise the name of the Lord’ (Psalm 148:4–5, same number in English; also quoted in 6.19). ‘The very heights of the heavens’ (πρὸς ἄκροις … τοῖς οὐρανοῖς) and ‘carried round by the revolving of heaven’ (περιφορά) echo Plato, Phaedrus 247b–c, where souls stand on the back of heaven and are carried round; an echo, not a quotation, so no inline Plato citation. Romans 1:20 LXX/NT τοῖς ποιήμασιν νοούμενα, matched. ‘The true disciple of Jesus’ = Paul. 1 Corinthians 13:10 has ὅταν δὲ ἔλθῃ; Origen has ἐάν.
